notes: The Hebrew title here is Adonai, “Lord”; verse 7 uses the divine name represented by LORD.
The heavenly throne scene follows the two kings sitting on their thrones in verse 10. The vision attributes the plan to entice Ahab and the lying spirit’s commission to the LORD.
The archer’s action can mean shooting innocently, unsuspectingly, or without a particular target. The exact parts of the armor named here are uncertain.
The Hebrew mentions prostitutes bathing at the pool. This detail is retained, as is Samaria’s location; the account is not rewritten to make every detail match the wording of the earlier oracle.
This public verse combines two Hebrew-numbered verses: Jehoshaphat’s conduct and the continuing high places. Subsequent public labels are one lower than the Hebrew labels.
The term for the male shrine attendants is traditionally rendered “male cult prostitutes.” Their exact activities are disputed; the term itself does not describe a sexual act.
The read tradition has Jehoshaphat “made” the ships; the written form differs. “Ships of Tarshish” can describe a class of trading vessels, without making Tarshish their destination.
vocabulary: The heavenly assembly attending the divine throne.
Local worship sites, often with altars; the term is not limited to mountaintops.
A source of gold named in the royal trading accounts; its location is uncertain.
